## Writing the independence claim {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/structured-data/09-math; notes-page: regression-models/structured-data.qmd; note-sha256: ea6228c13b9a3cdec00d2f961566e75429685fd5a720d40bc5e11310144a5495; role: math -->

A regression model without grouping terms often represents conditional independence as

$$
f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\prod_i f(y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A regression model without grouping terms often represents conditional independence as

$$
f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\prod_i f(y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1
https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116
:::

## Writing the independence claim

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/structured-data/10-concept; notes-page: regression-models/structured-data.qmd; note-sha256: ea6228c13b9a3cdec00d2f961566e75429685fd5a720d40bc5e11310144a5495; role: concept -->

Under this model, learning the residual for one row gives no information about the residual for another.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

After the predictors are known, the joint density is written as a product over trials. Under this model, learning the residual for one row gives no information about the residual for another.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1
https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116
:::

## Writing the independence claim

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/structured-data/11-concept; notes-page: regression-models/structured-data.qmd; note-sha256: ea6228c13b9a3cdec00d2f961566e75429685fd5a720d40bc5e11310144a5495; role: concept -->

Observing one trial can thus change what we expect for another trial that shares its participant or word.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

That claim is implausible here for two distinct reasons. Responses from one participant may resemble each other because that listener has a persistent response-speed baseline. Responses to one word may resemble each other because its acoustic and lexical properties are not completely represented by the measured predictors. Observing one trial can thus change what we expect for another trial that shares its participant or word.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1
https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116
:::

## Distinguishing crossed and nested units

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/structured-data/12-concept; notes-page: regression-models/structured-data.qmd; note-sha256: ea6228c13b9a3cdec00d2f961566e75429685fd5a720d40bc5e11310144a5495; role: concept -->

For instance, runs belong to participant sessions in the MALD release; a run identifier does not migrate between participants.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Participant and word are **crossed** because participants respond to many words and words receive responses from multiple participants. A nested structure would instead require each lower-level unit to belong to only one higher-level unit. For instance, runs belong to participant sessions in the MALD release; a run identifier does not migrate between participants.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1
https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116
:::

## Matching dependence to the claim

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/structured-data/14-concept; notes-page: regression-models/structured-data.qmd; note-sha256: ea6228c13b9a3cdec00d2f961566e75429685fd5a720d40bc5e11310144a5495; role: concept -->

More trials from the same participants or words improve estimates for those units but do not add participant or word replication.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A participant-population claim requires replication across participants. An item-population claim requires replication across words. A claim about both requires a design and analysis that preserve both sources. More trials from the same participants or words improve estimates for those units but do not add participant or word replication.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1
https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116
:::

## Matching dependence to the claim

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/structured-data/15-concept; notes-page: regression-models/structured-data.qmd; note-sha256: ea6228c13b9a3cdec00d2f961566e75429685fd5a720d40bc5e11310144a5495; role: concept -->

Mixed-effects models retain trial-level responses while representing both shared sources.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Averaging trials within participants would preserve participant replication while discarding word variation and within-participant trial predictors. Averaging within words would do the reverse. Mixed-effects models retain trial-level responses while representing both shared sources.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1
https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116
:::

## Matching dependence to the claim

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/structured-data/16-concept; notes-page: regression-models/structured-data.qmd; note-sha256: ea6228c13b9a3cdec00d2f961566e75429685fd5a720d40bc5e11310144a5495; role: concept -->

Before fitting one, record four facts.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Before fitting one, record four facts: (i) what one response row represents, (ii) which sampled units recur, (iii) whether those units are crossed or nested, and (iv) the populations across which the linguistic association should generalize. The next page translates those design facts into population coefficients and group distributions.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1
https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116
:::

## Beginning with the scientific target {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: math -->

The focal course model relates log response time to standardized log SUBTLEX frequency, standardized log acoustic duration, and standardized trial order. These predictors enter the population relation:

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\mathbf b]
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The focal course model relates log response time to standardized log SUBTLEX frequency, standardized log acoustic duration, and standardized trial order. These predictors enter the population relation:

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\mathbf b]
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Beginning with the scientific target

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: concept -->

In particular, $\beta_{\text{frequency}}$ is the expected change in log response time for a one-standard-deviation increase in log frequency, holding duration and trial order fixed.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Here $\boldsymbol\beta$ contains the population intercept and the three population associations. In particular, $\beta_{\text{frequency}}$ is the expected change in log response time for a one-standard-deviation increase in log frequency, holding duration and trial order fixed.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/05-concept; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: concept -->

It means that the coefficient is not itself indexed by a grouping level in this model.

## Representing sampled variation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/06-math; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: math -->

Participant $p$ receives an intercept deviation and a frequency-slope deviation:

$$
\mathbf b_p=
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0p}\\b_{1p}\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_p).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Participant $p$ receives an intercept deviation and a frequency-slope deviation:

$$
\mathbf b_p=
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0p}\\b_{1p}\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_p).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Representing sampled variation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: math -->

Word $w$ receives an intercept deviation,

$$
c_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),
$$

and the trial residual is

$$
\varepsilon_{pwi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Word $w$ receives an intercept deviation,

$$
c_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),
$$

and the trial residual is

$$
\varepsilon_{pwi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Representing sampled variation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/08-math; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: math -->

Combining the pieces gives

$$
Y_{pwi}
=\beta_0+\beta_f x_{wi}^{(f)}+\beta_d x_{wi}^{(d)}
+\beta_t x_{pwi}^{(t)}
+b_{0p}+b_{1p}x_{wi}^{(f)}+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Combining the pieces gives

$$
Y_{pwi}
=\beta_0+\beta_f x_{wi}^{(f)}+\beta_d x_{wi}^{(d)}
+\beta_t x_{pwi}^{(t)}
+b_{0p}+b_{1p}x_{wi}^{(f)}+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi}.
$$

## Representing sampled variation

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/09-concept; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: concept -->

Participant identity indexes deviations drawn from a population distribution.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The frequency column and participant identifier both enter the construction of the linear predictor, but they have different roles. Frequency is a measured predictor with a population coefficient. Participant identity indexes deviations drawn from a population distribution.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Fitting the MALD model

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/10-concept; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: concept -->

It is not a participant-specific slope or a causal effect of lexical frequency.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The fitted frequency coefficient is -0.031 log-response-time units per standard deviation. This is a population association conditional on duration and trial order. It is not a participant-specific slope or a causal effect of lexical frequency.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Storage type does not determine modeling role

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/fixed-and-random-effects/14-concept; notes-page: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: ec0282002d4a90c3e0af631f5f623c629a6cf1eba7b3e61e0edfa7a3f500902f; role: concept -->

A sampled identifier that records repeated observations can index remaining variation around that relation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Frequency, participant, item, and part of speech can all be stored as columns. Their storage types do not decide whether they receive population coefficients or group distributions. The decision follows the estimand and sampling design. A measured property that encodes a theoretical contrast belongs in the population relation. A sampled identifier that records repeated observations can index remaining variation around that relation.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Random effects and partial pooling

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: concept -->

A random-effects model represents the latter through a shared group distribution and **partial pooling**.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The preceding page separated population associations from variation across sampled listeners and words. A random-effects model represents the latter through a shared group distribution and **partial pooling**.

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: math -->

Y_{pwi}=\beta_0+b_p+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi},

c_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),\qquad
\varepsilon_{pwi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

## Model deviations from a shared center

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: concept -->

The parameters $\tau_p$ and $\tau_w$ describe the extent of persistent baseline differences.

::: {.notes}

The zero centers define $\beta_0$ as the population center. They do not assert that participants or words are identical. The parameters $\tau_p$ and $\tau_w$ describe the extent of persistent baseline differences.

## Comparing pooling strategies

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/05-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: concept -->

Partial pooling gives each participant a distinct deviation while estimating those deviations under one population distribution.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Complete pooling ignores participant identity and assigns every participant the population baseline $\beta_0$. No pooling estimates an unrelated mean for every participant. Partial pooling gives each participant a distinct deviation while estimating those deviations under one population distribution.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effects.qmd
:::

## Comparing pooling strategies {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/06-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: math -->

For a one-group normal random-intercept model with known variance components, the participant deviation has the form

$$
\widehat b_p
=w_p(\overline y_p-\beta_0),
$$

with

$$
w_p
=\frac{n_p\tau_p^2}{\sigma^2+n_p\tau_p^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a one-group normal random-intercept model with known variance components, the participant deviation has the form

$$
\widehat b_p
=w_p(\overline y_p-\beta_0),
$$

with

$$
w_p
=\frac{n_p\tau_p^2}{\sigma^2+n_p\tau_p^2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effects.qmd
:::

## Comparing pooling strategies

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: concept -->

Shrinkage is thus a consequence of the joint probability model, not a correction applied after fitting unrelated participant means.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The weight $w_p$ lies between zero and one. More observations or greater between-participant variation move it toward one; more within-participant residual variation moves it toward zero. Shrinkage is thus a consequence of the joint probability model, not a correction applied after fitting unrelated participant means.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effects.qmd
:::

## Keeping two kinds of variation separate

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/10-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: concept -->

One cannot substitute for the other: large residual variation is not persistent listener heterogeneity, and large group variation is not within-listener trial noise.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The participant standard deviation $\tau_p$ describes stable between-listener variation. The residual standard deviation $\sigma$ describes trial variation around participant and word baselines. One cannot substitute for the other: large residual variation is not persistent listener heterogeneity, and large group variation is not within-listener trial noise.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effects.qmd
:::

## Understanding exchangeability

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/11-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: concept -->

If listeners differ systematically by a measured property, that property should enter the population relation; the random effects then describe remaining variation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The shared normal distribution treats participant labels as exchangeable after conditioning on included predictors. Before observing the responses, swapping two arbitrary participant labels does not change the model. If listeners differ systematically by a measured property, that property should enter the population relation; the random effects then describe remaining variation.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effects.qmd
:::

## Understanding exchangeability

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effects/12-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 8f70e28396899fc77c58b90ebc352bc28eeec82c211a5b492c6b53da5d120f06; role: concept -->

The estimate, its conditional uncertainty, and the number of trials must be interpreted together.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An estimated deviation near zero can indicate either that a listener lies near the fitted center or that the listener's trials provide weak information and receive strong shrinkage. The estimate, its conditional uncertainty, and the number of trials must be interpreted together. The next page derives the dependence induced by the shared deviations.

## Random-intercept models

A **random-intercept model** places those deviations inside a regression equation.

## Inserting a participant deviation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-intercepts/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd; note-sha256: 3328e15dd418ec151338c218a7f0d3a9b17ed1f07b8d62816bf59827ec0e6322; role: math -->

For trial $i$ from participant $p$, a participant-intercept model has

$$
Y_{pi}=\beta_0+b_p+\mathbf x_{pi}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta+\varepsilon_{pi},
$$

with

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{pi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For trial $i$ from participant $p$, a participant-intercept model has

$$
Y_{pi}=\beta_0+b_p+\mathbf x_{pi}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta+\varepsilon_{pi},
$$

with

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{pi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd
:::

## Inserting a participant deviation

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-intercepts/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd; note-sha256: 3328e15dd418ec151338c218a7f0d3a9b17ed1f07b8d62816bf59827ec0e6322; role: concept -->

The deviation changes the vertical location of the participant's regression relation; it does not change any predictor association.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Participant $p$ has fitted baseline $\beta_0+b_p$. The deviation changes the vertical location of the participant's regression relation; it does not change any predictor association.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd

## Deriving the induced covariance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-intercepts/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd; note-sha256: 3328e15dd418ec151338c218a7f0d3a9b17ed1f07b8d62816bf59827ec0e6322; role: math -->

Two trials from the same participant share $b_p$:

$$
Y_{pi}=\beta_0+b_p+\varepsilon_{pi},
\qquad
Y_{pi'}=\beta_0+b_p+\varepsilon_{pi'}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Two trials from the same participant share $b_p$:

$$
Y_{pi}=\beta_0+b_p+\varepsilon_{pi},
\qquad
Y_{pi'}=\beta_0+b_p+\varepsilon_{pi'}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd
:::

## Deriving the induced covariance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-intercepts/06-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd; note-sha256: 3328e15dd418ec151338c218a7f0d3a9b17ed1f07b8d62816bf59827ec0e6322; role: math -->

Under independent residuals and independence between residuals and the group deviation,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{pi},Y_{pi'})
&=\operatorname{Cov}(b_p+\varepsilon_{pi},
                     b_p+\varepsilon_{pi'})\\
&=\operatorname{Var}[b_p]\\
&=\tau_p^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Under independent residuals and independence between residuals and the group deviation,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{pi},Y_{pi'})
&=\operatorname{Cov}(b_p+\varepsilon_{pi},
                     b_p+\varepsilon_{pi'})\\
&=\operatorname{Var}[b_p]\\
&=\tau_p^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd
:::

## Deriving the induced covariance

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-intercepts/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd; note-sha256: 3328e15dd418ec151338c218a7f0d3a9b17ed1f07b8d62816bf59827ec0e6322; role: concept -->

Marginally, before the deviation is known, the two responses are associated because they contain the same participant baseline.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Conditional on $b_p$, the residuals may be independent. Marginally, before the deviation is known, the two responses are associated because they contain the same participant baseline.

MALD trials also repeat spoken words. Give word $w$ a deviation $c_w$:

## Adding the crossed word intercept

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-intercepts/09-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-intercepts.qmd; note-sha256: 3328e15dd418ec151338c218a7f0d3a9b17ed1f07b8d62816bf59827ec0e6322; role: concept -->

Rows sharing both units have covariance $\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2$ under the model's independence assumptions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Two rows that share only a participant have covariance $\tau_p^2$. Two rows that share only a word have covariance $\tau_w^2$. Rows sharing both units have covariance $\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2$ under the model's independence assumptions.

## Intraclass correlation

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/intraclass-correlation/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd; note-sha256: c96e85742c64081124a6385871dc7900e6f45526dd69ba414df8cc9fb5ea5fcb; role: concept -->

The **intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)** summarizes the resulting correlation for a Gaussian random-intercept model.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The random-intercept page showed that responses sharing a participant or word also share a modeled deviation. The **intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)** summarizes the resulting correlation for a Gaussian random-intercept model.

## Deriving the crossed-unit correlations {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/intraclass-correlation/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd; note-sha256: c96e85742c64081124a6385871dc7900e6f45526dd69ba414df8cc9fb5ea5fcb; role: math -->

For the MALD intercept-only model,

$$
Y_{pwi}=\beta_0+b_p+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi},
$$

with independent components having variances $\tau_p^2$, $\tau_w^2$, and $\sigma^2$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For the MALD intercept-only model,

$$
Y_{pwi}=\beta_0+b_p+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi},
$$

with independent components having variances $\tau_p^2$, $\tau_w^2$, and $\sigma^2$.

## Deriving the crossed-unit correlations {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/intraclass-correlation/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd; note-sha256: c96e85742c64081124a6385871dc7900e6f45526dd69ba414df8cc9fb5ea5fcb; role: math -->

The marginal response variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pwi}]
=\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The marginal response variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pwi}]
=\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2.
$$

## Deriving the crossed-unit correlations {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/intraclass-correlation/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd; note-sha256: c96e85742c64081124a6385871dc7900e6f45526dd69ba414df8cc9fb5ea5fcb; role: math -->

Two distinct trials from the same participant but different words share only $b_p$, so their covariance is $\tau_p^2$. Their correlation is

$$
\rho_p
=\frac{\tau_p^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Two distinct trials from the same participant but different words share only $b_p$, so their covariance is $\tau_p^2$. Their correlation is

$$
\rho_p
=\frac{\tau_p^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd
:::

## Deriving the crossed-unit correlations {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/intraclass-correlation/06-math; notes-page: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd; note-sha256: c96e85742c64081124a6385871dc7900e6f45526dd69ba414df8cc9fb5ea5fcb; role: math -->

Two trials on the same word from different participants instead have

$$
\rho_w
=\frac{\tau_w^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Two trials on the same word from different participants instead have

$$
\rho_w
=\frac{\tau_w^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd
:::

## Deriving the crossed-unit correlations {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/intraclass-correlation/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd; note-sha256: c96e85742c64081124a6385871dc7900e6f45526dd69ba414df8cc9fb5ea5fcb; role: math -->

If two rows share both participant and word, the fitted correlation is

$$
\rho_{pw}
=\frac{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}
=\rho_p+\rho_w.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If two rows share both participant and word, the fitted correlation is

$$
\rho_{pw}
=\frac{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2}
{\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\sigma^2}
=\rho_p+\rho_w.
$$

## Relating the correlations to replication

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/intraclass-correlation/10-concept; notes-page: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd; note-sha256: c96e85742c64081124a6385871dc7900e6f45526dd69ba414df8cc9fb5ea5fcb; role: concept -->

Additional participants or words provide replication across the corresponding population.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Positive ICCs mean that repeated rows from one unit contain less independent information than the same number of rows from distinct units. Additional trials can estimate an observed participant's or word's baseline more precisely. Additional participants or words provide replication across the corresponding population.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd

## Keeping the interpretation model-specific

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/intraclass-correlation/11-concept; notes-page: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd; note-sha256: c96e85742c64081124a6385871dc7900e6f45526dd69ba414df8cc9fb5ea5fcb; role: concept -->

Logistic and Poisson mixed models require further scale choices because they do not estimate a Gaussian residual variance on the response scale.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Adding predictors can change every variance component. An intercept-only ICC and an ICC conditional on frequency, duration, and trial order need not agree. Random slopes also make the covariance depend on predictor values, so one constant ICC no longer describes every trial pair. Logistic and Poisson mixed models require further scale choices because they do not estimate a Gaussian residual variance on the response scale.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/intraclass-correlation.qmd

## Defining the conditional mode {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effect-estimates/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-effect-estimates.qmd; note-sha256: dc08f49812af572f399b255808282374c1fe8e033f62c7eb3c9c3b309ed42691; role: math -->

For participant $p$, collect the intercept and frequency-slope deviations in $\mathbf b_p$. Conditional on fitted population coefficients and variance components, the estimate is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf b}_p
=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\mathbf b_p}
\left{
\log f(\mathbf y_p\mid\mathbf b_p,\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\widehat\sigma)
+\log g(\mathbf b_p\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_p)
\right}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For participant $p$, collect the intercept and frequency-slope deviations in $\mathbf b_p$. Conditional on fitted population coefficients and variance components, the estimate is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf b}_p
=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\mathbf b_p}
\left{
\log f(\mathbf y_p\mid\mathbf b_p,\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\widehat\sigma)
+\log g(\mathbf b_p\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_p)
\right}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effect-estimates.qmd
:::

## Defining the conditional mode

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effect-estimates/05-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effect-estimates.qmd; note-sha256: dc08f49812af572f399b255808282374c1fe8e033f62c7eb3c9c3b309ed42691; role: concept -->

Their combination produces partial pooling.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The first term rewards values that fit the participant's trials. The second rewards values plausible under the estimated participant distribution. Their combination produces partial pooling.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effect-estimates.qmd

## Defining the conditional mode {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effect-estimates/06-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-effect-estimates.qmd; note-sha256: dc08f49812af572f399b255808282374c1fe8e033f62c7eb3c9c3b309ed42691; role: math -->

(\overline y_p-\beta_0).
$$

## Distinguishing deviations from group-specific coefficients {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effect-estimates/11-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-effect-estimates.qmd; note-sha256: dc08f49812af572f399b255808282374c1fe8e033f62c7eb3c9c3b309ed42691; role: math -->

`ranef(fit)` returns the deviations $\widehat b_{0p}$ and $\widehat b_{1p}$; `coef(fit)` adds the population coefficients.

The modes here describe modeled heterogeneity among sampled MALD listeners; they are not independently observed traits.

[Transcript]

Testing every conditional mode against zero would replace a population model with many separate hypotheses and would create a multiple-comparison problem. If a particular listener or dialect is a planned scientific target, that target should enter the population relation explicitly. A random-slope model also lets that association vary across participants.

## Adding a participant-specific association {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-slopes/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-slopes.qmd; note-sha256: 9290f600446a328032d1c847413189573040c4a45fb005ff39e841272ad687f0; role: math -->

For MALD trial $i$, participant $p$, and word $w$, write

$$
Y_{pwi}
=\beta_0+b_{0p}
+(\beta_f+b_{1p})x_{wi}^{(f)}
+\beta_d x_{wi}^{(d)}
+\beta_t x_{pwi}^{(t)}
+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For MALD trial $i$, participant $p$, and word $w$, write

$$
Y_{pwi}
=\beta_0+b_{0p}
+(\beta_f+b_{1p})x_{wi}^{(f)}
+\beta_d x_{wi}^{(d)}
+\beta_t x_{pwi}^{(t)}

$$

## Checking that the design contains the contrast

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-slopes/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-slopes.qmd; note-sha256: 9290f600446a328032d1c847413189573040c4a45fb005ff39e841272ad687f0; role: concept -->

A word has one lexical frequency, so repeated responses to that word cannot identify an item-specific frequency slope.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A participant-specific frequency association requires frequency variation within participants. A word has one lexical frequency, so repeated responses to that word cannot identify an item-specific frequency slope.

The data thus support participant frequency slopes but not word-specific frequency slopes.

## How the dependence changes {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-slopes/11-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-slopes.qmd; note-sha256: 9290f600446a328032d1c847413189573040c4a45fb005ff39e841272ad687f0; role: math -->

Two trials from participant $p$ share $b_{0p}$, and their covariance also contains the slope contribution

$$
x_{pwi}^{(f)}x_{pwi'}^{(f)}\tau_1^2
$$

plus intercept-slope covariance terms when the deviations are correlated.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Two trials from participant $p$ share $b_{0p}$, and their covariance also contains the slope contribution

$$
x_{pwi}^{(f)}x_{pwi'}^{(f)}\tau_1^2
$$

plus intercept-slope covariance terms when the deviations are correlated.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-slopes.qmd
:::

## How the dependence changes

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-slopes/12-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-slopes.qmd; note-sha256: 9290f600446a328032d1c847413189573040c4a45fb005ff39e841272ad687f0; role: concept -->

A constant participant ICC no longer summarizes every pair.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Trial pairs at different frequency values thus need not have the same covariance. A constant participant ICC no longer summarizes every pair.

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-slopes/13-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-slopes.qmd; note-sha256: 9290f600446a328032d1c847413189573040c4a45fb005ff39e841272ad687f0; role: concept -->

Its inclusion is licensed by both the within-participant frequency range and the goal of generalizing the frequency association across listeners.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The model still imposes one population frequency coefficient. The random slope states that this average is incomplete as a description of individual listeners. Its inclusion is licensed by both the within-participant frequency range and the goal of generalizing the frequency association across listeners. ## Writing one joint distribution {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effect-correlations/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-effect-correlations.qmd; note-sha256: 1c94e9a6ccda2dd627a96392b33330daaf6c642049789494aabe264a372b982a; role: math -->

For participant $p$, model

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
b_{0p}\\
b_{1p}
\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N
\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \rho\tau_0\tau_1\\
\rho\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2
\end{pmatrix}
\right).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For participant $p$, model

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
b_{0p}\\
b_{1p}
\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N
\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \rho\tau_0\tau_1\\
\rho\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2
\end{pmatrix}
\right).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effect-correlations.qmd

## Writing one joint distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effect-correlations/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effect-correlations.qmd; note-sha256: 1c94e9a6ccda2dd627a96392b33330daaf6c642049789494aabe264a372b982a; role: concept -->

The sign of *above* depends on the response and predictor coding.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The parameter $\rho$ is the correlation between participant intercept and frequency-slope deviations. A positive value means that participants above the population baseline tend to have frequency slopes above the population slope. The sign of *above* depends on the response and predictor coding.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/random-effect-correlations.qmd
:::

## Writing one joint distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effect-correlations/05-concept; notes-page: regression-models/random-effect-correlations.qmd; note-sha256: 1c94e9a6ccda2dd627a96392b33330daaf6c642049789494aabe264a372b982a; role: concept -->

It does not set either variance to zero; participants may still vary substantially in both dimensions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $\rho=0$, the model treats the deviations as uncorrelated. It does not set either variance to zero; participants may still vary substantially in both dimensions.

The fitted slope standard deviation is only 0.0121 log-response-time units, so a strong substantive story about the correlation would outrun the estimated slope variation.

## Why centering changes the correlation {.equation-slide}

$$
x_i^{c}=x_i-c.
$$

Because $x_i=x_i^c+c$, the group-specific part becomes

$$
b_{0p}+b_{1p}x_i
=(b_{0p}+cb_{1p})+b_{1p}x_i^c.
$$

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/random-effect-correlations/09-math; notes-page: regression-models/random-effect-correlations.qmd; note-sha256: 1c94e9a6ccda2dd627a96392b33330daaf6c642049789494aabe264a372b982a; role: math -->

$$

## Singular fits

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/singular-fits/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd; note-sha256: ce31e332c3d2d77fbf037d061e5cb5545cb5ea5cf186b208d84e309b3b895b33; role: concept -->

A **singular fit** occurs when the estimated covariance matrix has lower rank than the formula allows.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The random-effects-correlation page represented intercept and slope deviations with a covariance matrix. A **singular fit** occurs when the estimated covariance matrix has lower rank than the formula allows.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd
:::

## Rank and covariance dimensions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/singular-fits/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd; note-sha256: ce31e332c3d2d77fbf037d061e5cb5545cb5ea5cf186b208d84e309b3b895b33; role: math -->

Suppose a grouping term requests $q$ random-effect dimensions with covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$. A nonsingular fit requires

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)=q.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Suppose a grouping term requests $q$ random-effect dimensions with covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$. A nonsingular fit requires

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)=q.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd
:::

## Rank and covariance dimensions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/singular-fits/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd; note-sha256: ce31e332c3d2d77fbf037d061e5cb5545cb5ea5cf186b208d84e309b3b895b33; role: math -->

Writing the eigendecomposition as

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma
=\mathbf Q\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf Q^{\mathsf T},
$$

the rank is the number of positive eigenvalues in $\boldsymbol\Lambda$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Writing the eigendecomposition as

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma
=\mathbf Q\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf Q^{\mathsf T},
$$

the rank is the number of positive eigenvalues in $\boldsymbol\Lambda$.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd
:::

If one eigenvalue is zero, one linear combination of the requested deviations has no fitted variation and

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)<q.
$$

::: {.notes}

If one eigenvalue is zero, one linear combination of the requested deviations has no fitted variation and

In a larger structure, a collapsed dimension may involve a combination of several terms and may not be obvious from any one printed variance.

## Separating singularity from convergence

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/singular-fits/12-concept; notes-page: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd; note-sha256: ce31e332c3d2d77fbf037d061e5cb5545cb5ea5cf186b208d84e309b3b895b33; role: concept -->

`isSingular()` and the optimizer diagnostics answer different questions and both should be checked.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An optimizer can reach a boundary optimum successfully, producing a singular fit without a convergence failure. Conversely, a nonsingular covariance estimate can accompany an optimizer warning. `isSingular()` and the optimizer diagnostics answer different questions and both should be checked.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd
:::

## Separating singularity from convergence

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/singular-fits/13-concept; notes-page: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd; note-sha256: ce31e332c3d2d77fbf037d061e5cb5545cb5ea5cf186b208d84e309b3b895b33; role: concept -->

These moves encode different population assumptions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A singular fit should send us back to the design: which predictor contrasts vary within which groups, how many group levels support the covariance, and which population variation the scientific claim requires. Plausible responses include removing an unsupported correlation, removing an unsupported slope, collecting more within-group contrasts, or using a regularized model. These moves encode different population assumptions.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd
:::

## Separating singularity from convergence

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/singular-fits/14-concept; notes-page: regression-models/singular-fits.qmd; note-sha256: ce31e332c3d2d77fbf037d061e5cb5545cb5ea5cf186b208d84e309b3b895b33; role: concept -->

It is not a general stepwise-selection recipe, and it should not be used to search for a preferred fixed-effect conclusion.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The MALD revision above follows a predeclared design audit: it removes only the collapsed participant interaction slope. It is not a general stepwise-selection recipe, and it should not be used to search for a preferred fixed-effect conclusion. The next page carries the same group-variation logic to a binary linguistic response.

## Combining a Bernoulli response with group variation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models/06-math; notes-page: regression-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: 585684bbf1bec96cd42f51142000ddc240e13fdbdaf7ad06f6d16f26f687f37e; role: math -->

Let $Y_i=1$ when trial $i$ has an *in* response. Conditional on the random effects,

$$
Y_i\mid u_{p[i]},v_{w[i]},s_{q[i]}
\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)
=\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+u_{p[i]}+v_{w[i]}+s_{q[i]}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $Y_i=1$ when trial $i$ has an *in* response. Conditional on the random effects,

$$
Y_i\mid u_{p[i]},v_{w[i]},s_{q[i]}
\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)
=\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+u_{p[i]}+v_{w[i]}+s_{q[i]}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd
:::

The vector $\mathbf x_i$ contains verb class, contentfulness, and their interaction. Participant $p$, verb $w$, and sentence $q$ receive independent random intercepts:

$$
u_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2),\qquad
v_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),\qquad
s_q\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_q^2).
$$

## Conditional and population-averaged prediction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models/14-math; notes-page: regression-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: 585684bbf1bec96cd42f51142000ddc240e13fdbdaf7ad06f6d16f26f687f37e; role: math -->

Its variance is

$$
\tau_B^2=\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\tau_q^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A prediction at zero random effects is not generally the probability for a randomly drawn participant, verb, and sentence. Let $B$ be the sum of the three independent intercepts. Its variance is

$$
\tau_B^2=\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\tau_q^2.
$$

## Conditional and population-averaged prediction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models/15-math; notes-page: regression-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: 585684bbf1bec96cd42f51142000ddc240e13fdbdaf7ad06f6d16f26f687f37e; role: math -->

For fixed-effect location $\eta$, the random-effect-averaged probability is

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid\mathbf x)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta+b)
\phi(b;0,\tau_B^2)\,db.
$$

Because the inverse logit is nonlinear,

$$
\operatorname{E}_{B}
\left[\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta+B)\right]
\ne
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta)
$$

in general.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For fixed-effect location $\eta$, the random-effect-averaged probability is

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid\mathbf x)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta+b)
\phi(b;0,\tau_B^2)\,db.
$$

Because the inverse logit is nonlinear,

$$
\operatorname{E}_{B}
\left[\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta+B)\right]
\ne
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta)
$$

in general.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd
:::

An ordinal mixed model combines the cumulative link introduced for ordinal regression with the group deviations introduced for generalized linear mixed models.

## Ordinal mixed models

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: concept -->

We use **MegaVeridicality v1**, the *no*, *maybe*, and *yes* veridicality judgments described by White and Rawlins (2018) and distributed through the official MegaVeridicality project.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We use **MegaVeridicality v1**, the *no*, *maybe*, and *yes* veridicality judgments described by White and Rawlins (2018) and distributed through the official MegaVeridicality project. Each row records one response to a low-content sentence containing a clause-embedding verb. The direct task asks whether the embedded event happened after an assertion; the conditional task places that assertion in a conditional antecedent.

Treating the repeated numbers as the same people would invent a dependence relation not present in the study.

::: {.notes}

The two tasks recruited separate samples. Numeric participant labels recur across tasks, so the prepared table prefixes them with the task before constructing `respondent_id`. Treating the repeated numbers as the same people would invent a dependence relation not present in the study.

## A fixed teaching subset

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: concept -->

It retains all four polarity-by-task conditions for every selected verb and all 319 task-specific respondents.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The full active/native table contains 14951 responses from 375 active-frame verbs. Fitting the correlated-slope ordinal mixed model to that table makes routine course builds unnecessarily slow. We therefore use a fixed teaching subset: all 2990 responses for the 75 verbs assigned to fold 1 by the release’s salted verb-hash partition. The partition was constructed without reference to the response values. It retains all four polarity-by-task conditions for every selected verb and all 319 task-specific respondents.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## A fixed teaching subset

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: concept -->

The model also analyzes raw ordered responses; it does not reproduce White and Rawlins's participant-threshold normalization, derived veridicality and factivity measures, or responsivity analysis.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This is a computational teaching subset, not a probability sample from the English clause-embedding lexicon. The estimates describe the selected verbs and should not be reported as full-data estimates. The model also analyzes raw ordered responses; it does not reproduce White and Rawlins's participant-threshold normalization, derived veridicality and factivity measures, or responsivity analysis.

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf

## Retaining the ordered response {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/08-math; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: math -->

For response $Y_i$ and cutpoint $c$, the cumulative-logit model is

$$
\operatorname{logit}\mathbb{P}(Y_i\le c)
=\kappa_c-\eta_i,
\qquad c\in\{1,2\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For response $Y_i$ and cutpoint $c$, the cumulative-logit model is

$$
\operatorname{logit}\mathbb{P}(Y_i\le c)
=\kappa_c-\eta_i,
\qquad c\in\{1,2\}.
$$

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## Retaining the ordered response {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/09-math; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: math -->

The location predictor is

$$
\eta_i
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_{v[i]}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b_{v[i]}
+u_{r[i]}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The location predictor is

$$
\eta_i
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_{v[i]}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b_{v[i]}
+u_{r[i]}.
$$

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## Retaining the ordered response {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/10-math; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: math -->

The fixed part contains polarity, task, and their interaction. Verbs receive correlated intercept, polarity-slope, and task-slope deviations; respondents receive intercept deviations. For verb $v$ and respondent $r$,

$$
\mathbf b_v\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_v),
\qquad
u_r\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_r^2).
$$

With logistic cumulative distribution $F$, the three category probabilities are

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{no})=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{maybe})
=F(\kappa_2-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(\kappa_2-\eta_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The fixed part contains polarity, task, and their interaction. Verbs receive correlated intercept, polarity-slope, and task-slope deviations; respondents receive intercept deviations. For verb $v$ and respondent $r$,

$$
\mathbf b_v\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_v),
\qquad
u_r\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_r^2).
$$

With logistic cumulative distribution $F$, the three category probabilities are

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{no})=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{maybe})
=F(\kappa_2-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(\kappa_2-\eta_i).
$$

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## Stating which groups are represented in a prediction

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/15-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: concept -->

A prediction for a new respondent and new verb must handle both group distributions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A prediction for an observed respondent and verb can condition on both estimated deviations. A prediction for a new respondent judging an observed verb may condition on the verb deviation but cannot reuse an observed respondent effect. A prediction for a new respondent and new verb must handle both group distributions.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## Stating which groups are represented in a prediction

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/16-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: concept -->

A reported probability must thus state which groups are represented in the target.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Setting both deviations to zero gives a location at the center of the link-scale distributions, as in the figure. Averaging category probabilities over either distribution generally produces different response-scale probabilities because the inverse cumulative-logit transformation is nonlinear. A reported probability must thus state which groups are represented in the target.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## What the fitted location can and cannot represent

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/17-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: concept -->

It changes category probabilities; it does not add a fixed number of slider points.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A positive location shift moves probability toward higher ordered responses. It changes category probabilities; it does not add a fixed number of slider points.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## What the fitted location can and cannot represent

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/18-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: concept -->

A location-intercept model leaves those possibilities outside its structure.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The verb random slopes allow the polarity and task associations to vary across observed verbs. The respondent random intercept allows overall response location to vary across respondents. It cannot represent every response style: respondents might also differ in threshold spacing or in how often they use *maybe*. A location-intercept model leaves those possibilities outside its structure.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## What the fitted location can and cannot represent

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/ordinal-mixed-models/19-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: bcc704d28c76c2941e470f4c2d0345073767ef9fd819ed1786d77e9bfcd88233; role: concept -->

The next worked page asks whether the fixed interaction predicts judgments for verbs absent from fitting.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

White and Rawlins normalize responses and study derived veridicality, factivity, responsivity, and clause-selection patterns. The course model instead analyzes raw ordered responses as a function of polarity and task. It is related to the source design, but it is not a reproduction of the paper's normalization or responsivity analysis. The next worked page asks whether the fixed interaction predicts judgments for verbs absent from fitting.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/

## From ordered responses to a likelihood {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/aspectual-similarity-example/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/aspectual-similarity-example.qmd; note-sha256: 22dd77937802867412f669aa626231cd566da5160b57a599fa94615d50c249cf; role: math -->

For ordered category $k$ and fixed-effect location $\eta_i$, define

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=k\mid\mathbf x_i)
=F(\kappa_k-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_{k-1}-\eta_i),
$$

where $F$ is the logistic cumulative distribution, $\kappa_0=-\infty$, and $\kappa_3=\infty$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For ordered category $k$ and fixed-effect location $\eta_i$, define

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=k\mid\mathbf x_i)
=F(\kappa_k-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_{k-1}-\eta_i),
$$

where $F$ is the logistic cumulative distribution, $\kappa_0=-\infty$, and $\kappa_3=\infty$.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf

## From ordered responses to a likelihood {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/aspectual-similarity-example/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/aspectual-similarity-example.qmd; note-sha256: 22dd77937802867412f669aa626231cd566da5160b57a599fa94615d50c249cf; role: math -->

The likelihood is

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\kappa)
=\prod_i\mathbb{P}(Y_i=y_i\mid\mathbf x_i),
$$

and its mean log score on held-out judgments is

$$
\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{i\in\mathrm{test}}
\log\mathbb{P}(Y_i=y_i\mid\mathbf x_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The likelihood is

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\kappa)
=\prod_i\mathbb{P}(Y_i=y_i\mid\mathbf x_i),
$$

and its mean log score on held-out judgments is

$$

\sum_{i\in\mathrm{test}}

## The Laplace approximation

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: concept -->

A likelihood for the observed responses must thus average over every possible random-effect value.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A generalized linear mixed model contains random effects that are not observed directly. The response likelihood is conditional on their values, and the model assigns those values a population distribution. A likelihood for the observed responses must thus average over every possible random-effect value.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## The Laplace approximation

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: concept -->

We expose that computation with one participant intercept from the SuperTelicity release introduced on the GLMM page.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This integral usually has no elementary form for a logistic mixed model. The **Laplace approximation** replaces the log integrand with a quadratic near its highest point. We expose that computation with one participant intercept from the SuperTelicity release introduced on the GLMM page.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Why the integral appears {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: math -->

For participant $p$, let $\mathbf y_p$ denote the binary preposition choices and $b_p$ the participant intercept. Conditional on $b_p$, the participant likelihood is

$$
p(\mathbf y_p\mid b_p,\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For participant $p$, let $\mathbf y_p$ denote the binary preposition choices and $b_p$ the participant intercept. Conditional on $b_p$, the participant likelihood is

$$
p(\mathbf y_p\mid b_p,\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Why the integral appears {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: math -->

The group model supplies the density $f_B(b_p\mid\tau)$. The observed-data contribution is

$$
p(\mathbf y_p\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\tau)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
p(\mathbf y_p\mid b_p,\boldsymbol\beta)
f_B(b_p\mid\tau)\,db_p.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The group model supplies the density $f_B(b_p\mid\tau)$. The observed-data contribution is

$$
p(\mathbf y_p\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\tau)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
p(\mathbf y_p\mid b_p,\boldsymbol\beta)
f_B(b_p\mid\tau)\,db_p.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Why the integral appears

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: concept -->

Selecting only the best-fitting intercept would omit uncertainty about that latent value.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Integration adds support over every intercept value. Selecting only the best-fitting intercept would omit uncertainty about that latent value.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Expanding the log integrand {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: math -->

Define

$$
h(b)
=\log p(\mathbf y_p\mid b,\boldsymbol\beta)
+\log f_B(b\mid\tau).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Define

$$
h(b)
=\log p(\mathbf y_p\mid b,\boldsymbol\beta)
+\log f_B(b\mid\tau).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Expanding the log integrand {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/08-math; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: math -->

Let $\widehat b$ maximize $h(b)$. At the mode,

$$
h'(\widehat b)=0.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $\widehat b$ maximize $h(b)$. At the mode,

$$
h'(\widehat b)=0.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Expanding the log integrand {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/09-math; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: math -->

The second-order Taylor expansion is

$$
h(b)
\approx h(\widehat b)
+h'(\widehat b)(b-\widehat b)
+\frac{1}{2}h''(\widehat b)(b-\widehat b)^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The second-order Taylor expansion is

$$
h(b)
\approx h(\widehat b)
+h'(\widehat b)(b-\widehat b)
+\frac{1}{2}h''(\widehat b)(b-\widehat b)^2.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Expanding the log integrand {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/10-math; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: math -->

The first-derivative term vanishes at the mode. Writing

$$
H=-h''(\widehat b)>0
$$

gives

$$
h(b)
\approx h(\widehat b)-\frac{H}{2}(b-\widehat b)^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The first-derivative term vanishes at the mode. Writing

$$
H=-h''(\widehat b)>0
$$

gives

$$
h(b)
\approx h(\widehat b)-\frac{H}{2}(b-\widehat b)^2.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Expanding the log integrand {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/11-math; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: math -->

Exponentiating produces a normal-shaped approximation whose integral is

$$
\int \exp\{h(b)\}\,db
\approx
\exp\{h(\widehat b)\}
\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{H}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Exponentiating produces a normal-shaped approximation whose integral is

$$
\int \exp\{h(b)\}\,db
\approx
\exp\{h(\widehat b)\}
\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{H}}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

## Expanding the log integrand {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/laplace-approximation/12-math; notes-page: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd; note-sha256: d1cc3c54c0215e57a6140e20d3c344098d10de412657916cdabe389100ead198; role: math -->

Equivalently,

$$
\log L
\approx h(\widehat b)
+\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi)
-\frac{1}{2}\log H.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Equivalently,

$$
\log L
\approx h(\widehat b)
+\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi)
-\frac{1}{2}\log H.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/laplace-approximation.qmd
:::

Sparse groups, rare responses, boundary variances, or strong asymmetry may make the local quadratic less adequate.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The approximation is a computational method, not a new response model. It does not add a predictor, repair a missing random slope, or make an inappropriate link valid. It tends to be most accurate when the integrand is concentrated and roughly symmetric near its mode; sparse groups, rare responses, boundary variances, or strong asymmetry may make the local quadratic less adequate.

## Stating the observation and target

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/poisson-mixed-models/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/poisson-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: 72f2b1d8bf42cef89aa52f94318b14743bcd6c0987ae9af92117adecc66ab73b; role: concept -->

A remote reference to an existing node does not create another Scene.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

One row is one complete passage graph in English or French. `pair_id` joins the aligned translations. `word_count` is the number of annotated words, and `scene_count` counts distinct nodes with an outgoing Process or State edge. A remote reference to an existing node does not create another Scene.

[Sources]

## Stating the observation and target

It is a rate per annotated word, not a contrast in raw counts.

::: {.notes}

## Assembling the conditional model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/poisson-mixed-models/08-math; notes-page: regression-models/poisson-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: 72f2b1d8bf42cef89aa52f94318b14743bcd6c0987ae9af92117adecc66ab73b; role: math -->

For passage pair $p$ and language side $l$,

$$
Y_{pl}\mid b_p
\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{pl}),
$$

with probability mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_{pl}=y\mid b_p)
=\frac{\exp(-\lambda_{pl})\lambda_{pl}^{y}}{y!}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For passage pair $p$ and language side $l$,

$$
Y_{pl}\mid b_p
\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{pl}),
$$

with probability mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_{pl}=y\mid b_p)
=\frac{\exp(-\lambda_{pl})\lambda_{pl}^{y}}{y!}.
$$

[Sources]

https://aclanthology.org/W15-3502/
https://aclanthology.org/P13-1023/

## Assembling the conditional model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/poisson-mixed-models/09-math; notes-page: regression-models/poisson-mixed-models.qmd; note-sha256: 72f2b1d8bf42cef89aa52f94318b14743bcd6c0987ae9af92117adecc66ab73b; role: math -->

The log expected count combines word exposure, a language contrast, and the pair intercept:

$$
\log\lambda_{pl}
=\log W_{pl}
+\beta_0
+\beta_1\operatorname{French}_{pl}
+b_p,
$$

where

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The log expected count combines word exposure, a language contrast, and the pair intercept:

$$
\log\lambda_{pl}
=\log W_{pl}
+\beta_0
+\beta_1\operatorname{French}_{pl}
+b_p,
$$

where

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2).
$$

## Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: concept -->

A Poisson regression without that structure can appear overdispersed because it combines low-rate and high-rate pairs under one mean.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The Poisson mixed-model page supplied one source of structured count variation: persistent differences across aligned passage pairs. A Poisson regression without that structure can appear overdispersed because it combines low-rate and high-rate pairs under one mean.

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: concept -->

The distinction follows from the law of total variance.

## Beginning with the conditional Poisson claim {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: math -->

For language side $l$ of passage pair $p$, write

$$
Y_{pl}\mid b_p
\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{pl}(b_p)),
$$

with

$$
\lambda_{pl}(b_p)
=\lambda_{pl}^{(0)}\exp(b_p),
$$

where

$$
\lambda_{pl}^{(0)}
=W_{pl}\exp\left(
\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{French}_{pl}
\right)
$$

is the expected count when the pair deviation is zero, and

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For language side $l$ of passage pair $p$, write

$$

## Averaging over the passage-pair population {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: math -->

For a new aligned pair, the marginal mean is

$$
m_{pl}
=\operatorname{E}_{b}\left[\lambda_{pl}(b)\right].
$$

Because $b\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2)$,

$$
\operatorname{E}[\exp(b)]
=\exp\left(\frac{\tau_p^2}{2}\right),
$$

so

$$
m_{pl}
=\lambda_{pl}^{(0)}
\exp\left(\frac{\tau_p^2}{2}\right).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a new aligned pair, the marginal mean is

$$
m_{pl}
=\operatorname{E}_{b}\left[\lambda_{pl}(b)\right].
$$

Because $b\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2)$,

$$
\operatorname{E}[\exp(b)]
=\exp\left(\frac{\tau_p^2}{2}\right),
$$

so

$$
m_{pl}
=\lambda_{pl}^{(0)}
\exp\left(\frac{\tau_p^2}{2}\right).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Averaging over the passage-pair population {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/08-math; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: math -->

The law of total variance gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}]
&=\operatorname{E}_{b}
  [\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}\mid b]]
  +\operatorname{Var}_{b}
  [\mathbb{E}[Y_{pl}\mid b]]\\
&=\operatorname{E}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]
  +\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]\\
&=m_{pl}+\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)].
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The law of total variance gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}]
&=\operatorname{E}_{b}
  [\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}\mid b]]
  +\operatorname{Var}_{b}
  [\mathbb{E}[Y_{pl}\mid b]]\\
&=\operatorname{E}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]
  +\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]\\
&=m_{pl}+\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)].
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Averaging over the passage-pair population {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/09-math; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: math -->

The lognormal moment identity yields

$$
\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]
=m_{pl}^2\left[\exp(\tau_p^2)-1\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The lognormal moment identity yields

$$
\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]
=m_{pl}^2\left[\exp(\tau_p^2)-1\right].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Averaging over the passage-pair population {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/10-math; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: math -->

Thus,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}]
=m_{pl}
+m_{pl}^2\left[\exp(\tau_p^2)-1\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}]
=m_{pl}
+m_{pl}^2\left[\exp(\tau_p^2)-1\right].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/11-concept; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: concept -->

Marginal variance then exceeds marginal mean even though every conditional count distribution is Poisson.

## Substituting the fitted UCCA pair variance

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/12-concept; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: concept -->

The resulting marginal variance-to-mean ratio is 1.254.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

At the observed-data fit, the population-center mean for an English passage with 100 annotated words is 16.93 Scenes. Averaging over new passage-pair heterogeneity raises the mean to 17.06 and gives marginal variance 21.40. The resulting marginal variance-to-mean ratio is 1.254.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd

## Diagnosing conditional fit

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/14-concept; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: concept -->

A Pearson diagnostic assesses that different question.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The marginal moment identity does not tell us whether the conditional Poisson variance fits the observed within-model residual pattern. A Pearson diagnostic assesses that different question.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Diagnosing conditional fit

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/16-concept; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: concept -->

The two claims refer to different conditioning levels and can hold simultaneously.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The conditional Pearson ratio is 0.445, which is below one. These data are conditionally underdispersed relative to the fitted Poisson working model even though the pair intercept induces extra-Poisson *marginal* variance. The two claims refer to different conditioning levels and can hold simultaneously.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Diagnosing conditional fit

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/17-concept; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: concept -->

A negative-binomial or observation-level dispersion term can change count variance but does not by itself encode this paired association.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Two sides of the same passage pair share $b_p$. After that effect is averaged out, a high count on one side provides information that the pair has a high baseline, which in turn raises the expectation for the other side. A negative-binomial or observation-level dispersion term can change count variance but does not by itself encode this paired association.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd
:::

## Diagnosing conditional fit

<!-- generated-slide-id: mixed-effects-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects/18-concept; notes-page: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 03e126bb14ea286fc63e59ac38a5b02b4a81bc58c2720bdf666dc2098ee99ffb; role: concept -->

Remaining conditional underdispersion, omitted predictors, varying associations, or another response family require separate model criticism.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Random intercepts thus do not repair every dispersion pattern. They are licensed by a known repeated unit and explain one structured source of variation. Remaining conditional underdispersion, omitted predictors, varying associations, or another response family require separate model criticism.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd
:::
